description:
She posed as the slaveholder. He posed as her enslaved servant.

Ellen and William Craft’s 1848 escape depended on more than disguise: they had to navigate the vulnerabilities their assumed identities created. What happens when the supposed master cannot sign—and appearance is not proof of ownership?

Detailed Baltimore checkpoint events are reported in William Craft’s later 1860 account. A report published weeks after the escape supports the bound-hand/signature explanation; it was not an eyewitness account of the journey.

Archival portraits and original explanatory graphics; no escape footage. AI-generated narration.

#History #EllenAndWilliamCraft #Magnivis
firstComment: The evidence has layers: Brown’s January 1849 letter reports the injured-hand/signature strategy after meeting the Crafts. William’s 1860 book supplies the detailed Baltimore account. Neither is a contemporaneous recording of the checkpoint. Their escape succeeded; later contemporary reporting documents the 1850 recapture attempt in Boston. Sources: William Craft’s 1860 account https://docsouth.unc.edu/neh/craft/craft.html ; Brown’s near-contemporary report (Liberator,Jan 12, 1849) https://fair-use.org/the-liberator/1849/01/12/the-liberator-19-02.pdf ; contemporary Boston report (Nov 1, 1850) https://fair-use.org/the-liberator/1850/11/01/the-liberator-20-44.pdf ; NPS synthesis https://www.nps.gov/articles/-a-desperate-leap-for-liberty-the-escape-of-william-and-ellen-craft.htm
